proofs.proof_tex:
Lemma~\ref{lem:classical-johnson-decomposition} supplies the orthogonal Johnson-degree decomposition of the uniform slice.  Let \(\mathsf A_n\) denote the unnormalized adjacency operator of the Kneser graph on \(\Omega_{n,M}\).  By Lemma~\ref{lem:classical-kneser-spectrum}, its eigenvalue on \(\mathcal H_{n,k}\) is
\[
 \mu_{n,k}=(-1)^k\binom{n-M-k}{M-k}.
\]
Every vertex has \(\binom{n-M}{M}\) disjoint neighbors, so Definition~\ref{def:kneser-covariance} gives \(\mathsf K_n=\binom{n-M}{M}^{-1}\mathsf A_n\).  Since \(n\ge 2M\), all factorials below are defined, and hence
\[
 \lambda_{n,k}
 =\frac{\mu_{n,k}}{\binom{n-M}{M}}
 =(-1)^k\frac{M!}{(M-k)!}\frac{(n-M-k)!}{(n-M)!}
 =(-1)^k\frac{(M)_k}{(n-M)_k}.
\]
The disjointness relation is symmetric and the slice law is uniform, so \(\mathsf K_n\) is self-adjoint under \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_n\).  If \(f\) and \(g\) are centered, Definition~\ref{def:johnson-decomposition}, orthogonality of the \(\mathcal H_{n,k}\), and the displayed eigenvalue give
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(f(A),g(C))
 =\langle f,\mathsf K_ng\rangle_n
 =\sum_{k=1}^M\lambda_{n,k}
   \langle\Pi_{n,k}f,\Pi_{n,k}g\rangle_n.
\]
Apply this identity to each ordered pair \((h_{a,n}^{\circ},h_{b,n}^{\circ})\).  Self-adjointness gives \(C_{01,n}=C_{10,n}\), while linearity of \(\Pi_{n,k}\) gives
\[
 C_{11,n}+C_{00,n}-2C_{10,n}
 =\sum_{k=1}^M\lambda_{n,k}
   \|\Pi_{n,k}(h_{1,n}-h_{0,n})\|_n^2.
\]
This is the asserted formula for \(C_{\tau\tau,n}\).

Write \(q_n=1-p_n=G_{0n}/G_n\) and \(x_{zg}=h_{z,n}^{\circ}(A_{ng})\).  Each \(A_{ng}\) is uniform on \(\Omega_{n,M}\), each \(Z_{ng}\) has mean \(p_n\), and the two randomizations are independent by Definition~\ref{def:random-partition-design}.  Therefore Definition~\ref{def:pame-estimator} yields
\[
 \mathbb E\widehat\tau_n
 =\mathbb E_nh_{1,n}-\mathbb E_nh_{0,n}=\tau_n
\]
and
\[
 \widehat\tau_n-\tau_n
 =\frac1{G_n}\sum_{g=1}^{G_n}
 \left\{\frac{Z_{ng}}{p_n}x_{1g}
 -\frac{1-Z_{ng}}{q_n}x_{0g}\right\}.
\]
The diagonal terms in the second moment of this sum equal \(R_n/G_n\).  For distinct \(g,g'\), complete randomization gives
\[
 \frac{\mathbb E(Z_{ng}Z_{ng'})}{p_n^2}
 =\frac{G_n(G_{1n}-1)}{G_{1n}(G_n-1)},\qquad
 \frac{\mathbb E((1-Z_{ng})(1-Z_{ng'}))}{q_n^2}
 =\frac{G_n(G_{0n}-1)}{G_{0n}(G_n-1)},
\]
and
\[
 \frac{\mathbb E(Z_{ng}(1-Z_{ng'}))}{p_nq_n}
 =\frac{G_n}{G_n-1}.
\]
The corresponding group pairs are uniform ordered disjoint pairs, so Definition~\ref{def:kneser-covariance} identifies their products with \(C_{ab,n}\).  Summing the \(G_n(G_n-1)\) ordered off-diagonal terms and using \(C_{01,n}=C_{10,n}\), proved in Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-kneser-identity}, gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sigma_n^2
 &=\frac{R_n}{G_n}
   +\frac{G_{1n}-1}{G_{1n}}C_{11,n}
   +\frac{G_{0n}-1}{G_{0n}}C_{00,n}-2C_{10,n}\\
 &=\frac{R_n}{G_n}+C_{\tau\tau,n}
   -\frac{C_{11,n}}{G_{1n}}-\frac{C_{00,n}}{G_{0n}}.
 \end{aligned}
\]

For the CR2 expectation, let \(X_1,\ldots,X_m\) be the observed group means in arm \(z\), where \(m=G_{zn}\).  Marginally \(\operatorname{Var}(X_j)=V_{z,n}\) and, for \(j\ne\ell\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_j,X_\ell)=C_{zz,n}\).  Expanding the denominator-\(m-1\) sample variance gives
\[
 \mathbb E s_{z,n}^2
 =\frac1{m-1}\left\{mV_{z,n}-m\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)\right\}
 =V_{z,n}-C_{zz,n}.
\]
Division by \(G_{1n}\) and \(G_{0n}\) proves the asserted expectation formula.  Finally, \(R_n/G_n=V_{1,n}/G_{1n}+V_{0,n}/G_{0n}\); subtracting the exact variance identity therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb E\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}-\sigma_n^2=-C_{\tau\tau,n}.
\]

Bounded potential outcomes imply \(|h_{z,n}|\le B\), hence \(V_{z,n}\le B^2\) and
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^M\|\Pi_{n,k}(h_{1,n}-h_{0,n})\|_n^2
 =\operatorname{Var}_n(h_{1,n}-h_{0,n})\le4B^2.
\]
Because \(M\) is fixed and \(G_n\to\infty\), the constraint \(MG_n\le n\) implies \(n\to\infty\).  Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-kneser-identity} gives
\[
 G_n\lambda_{n,1}=-\frac{MG_n}{n-M}=-\frac{N_n}{n-M}\longrightarrow-\rho
\]
by Assumption~\ref{ass:sampling-fraction}.  For every \(k\ge2\), the explicit falling-factorial formula and fixed \(M\) give \(|\lambda_{n,k}|\le K_Mn^{-k}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).  Since \(G_n\le n/M\),
\[
 \left|G_n\sum_{k=2}^M\lambda_{n,k}
 \|\Pi_{n,k}(h_{1,n}-h_{0,n})\|_n^2\right|
 \le \frac{4B^2K_M}{M n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus \(G_nC_{\tau\tau,n}+\rho E_{\tau,1,n}\to0\), uniformly over schedules obeying the common bound \(B\).

For a centered \(f\), the spectral identity and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 |\langle f,\mathsf K_nf\rangle_n|
 \le \max_{1\le k\le M}|\lambda_{n,k}|\,\|f\|_n^2.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(n\), the maximum is at most \(K_M/n\).  Consequently \(|C_{zz,n}|\le K_MB^2/n\).  Assumption~\ref{ass:stable-treatment-fraction} keeps \(p_n\) and \(1-p_n\) bounded away from zero, so
\[
 \frac{C_{11,n}}{p_n}+\frac{C_{00,n}}{1-p_n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Multiplying Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-pame-variance} by \(G_n\) now yields
\[
 G_n\sigma_n^2
 =R_n+G_nC_{\tau\tau,n}
 -\frac{C_{11,n}}{p_n}-\frac{C_{00,n}}{1-p_n}
 =R_n-\rho E_{\tau,1,n}+o(1).
\]
The nondegeneracy assumption is not needed for this algebraic limit; it is used later for studentization and the martingale Lindeberg bound.

Put \(T_n=\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n\).  Assumption~\ref{ass:stable-treatment-fraction} supplies \(\eta>0\) such that \(G_{1n},G_{0n}\ge\eta G_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).

First consider a unit-reveal time.  Given two possible values for the next unit, couple the two uniform conditional tails by transposing those two units and leaving all other permutation entries and the label permutation unchanged.  A transposition changes at most two completed \(M\)-blocks, including when one transposed entry lies beyond the first \(N_n\) positions.  Each changed group mean remains in \([-B,B]\) by Assumption~\ref{ass:bounded-potential-outcomes}; hence the two coupled terminal values of \(T_n\) differ by at most
\[
 2(2B)\max(G_{1n}^{-1},G_{0n}^{-1})\le \frac{4B}{\eta G_n}.
\]
The conditional expectation after revealing the next unit therefore ranges over an interval of this length.  Its difference from its conditional average at the preceding time, namely \(D_{n,r}\), has no larger absolute value.

At a label-reveal time, couple the two possible next labels by swapping the current label with a future occurrence of the opposite label.  At most two groups switch arms.  Switching one group changes the estimator by at most \(B(G_{1n}^{-1}+G_{0n}^{-1})\), so here
\[
 |D_{n,r}|\le 2B(G_{1n}^{-1}+G_{0n}^{-1})
 \le\frac{4B}{\eta G_n}.
\]
At a time when only one label is possible the increment is zero.  Thus the claimed bound holds with, for example, \(K=4B/\eta\), which depends only on \(B\) and the limiting allocation \(p\) (and hence is admissibly denoted \(K(B,M,p)\)).

Assumption~\ref{ass:scaled-variance-nondegeneracy} gives \(\sigma_n\ge\sqrt{c_\sigma/(2G_n)}\) eventually.  Therefore
\[
 \frac{\max_r|D_{n,r}|}{\sigma_n}
 \le K\sqrt{\frac{2}{c_\sigma G_n}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
For fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), the event \(|D_{n,r}|>\varepsilon\sigma_n\) is consequently empty for every \(r\) and every sufficiently large \(n\).  The displayed conditional Lindeberg sum is then identically zero, proving the last assertion.

The terminal sigma-field in Definition~\ref{def:reveal-martingale} reveals both randomizations, while \(\mathcal F_{n,0}\) is trivial.  Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-pame-variance} gives \(\mathbb E(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)=0\); hence the Doob decomposition telescopes to
\[
 \sum_{r=1}^{N_n+G_n}D_{n,r}=\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n.
\]
Membership in \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{dense}}\) includes Assumption~\ref{ass:predictable-variance-stability}, namely \(Q_n/\sigma_n^2\xrightarrow{p}1\).  Lemma~\ref{lem:reveal-increment-bound} proves, from boundedness, stable arm fractions, and scaled-variance nondegeneracy, the conditional Lindeberg condition for \(D_{n,r}/\sigma_n\).  All increments are square integrable because they are bounded.  Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale-array-clt} therefore applies and yields
\[
 \frac{\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n}{\sigma_n}\rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,1).
\]
The probability law here is solely the design law of \((\mathbf A_n,\mathbf Z_n)\); the schedule \(Y_{i,n}(z,A)\) was held fixed throughout.

Fix an arm \(z\), put \(m=G_{zn}\), and let \(f\) be either \(h_{z,n}\) or \(h_{z,n}^2\).  The arm's \(m\) realized groups form an exchangeable ordered disjoint sample.  Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\left(\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^mf(A_j)\right)
 =\frac{V_n(f)}m+\frac{m-1}{m}C_n(f,f),
\]
where \(V_n(f)=\operatorname{Var}_n(f(A))\).  The left side is nonnegative, and the spectral bound used in Theorem~\ref{thm:dense-projection-limit} gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\left(\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^mf(A_j)\right)
 \le \frac{V_n(f)}m+|C_n(f,f)|
 \le \frac{V_n(f)}m+\frac{K_MV_n(f)}n.
\]
Here \(m\asymp G_n\), \(G_n\le n/M\), and \(|h_{z,n}|\le B\), so the right side is \(O(G_n^{-1})\), also for \(f=h_{z,n}^2\).  Chebyshev's inequality thus shows that the empirical first and second moments in each arm converge in probability to their slice counterparts.  Since \(m\to\infty\), the identity
\[
 s_{z,n}^2=\frac{m}{m-1}\left\{m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^mf(A_j)^2-\left(m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^mf(A_j)\right)^2\right\}
\]
with \(f=h_{z,n}\) gives \(s_{z,n}^2-V_{z,n}\xrightarrow{p}0\).  Hence
\[
 G_n\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}
 =\frac{s_{1,n}^2}{p_n}+\frac{s_{0,n}^2}{1-p_n}
 =R_n+o_p(1).
\]
Combining this with Theorem~\ref{thm:dense-projection-limit} proves
\[
 G_n(\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}-\sigma_n^2)
 -\rho E_{\tau,1,n}\xrightarrow{p}0.
\]

Let \(D_n=R_n-\rho E_{\tau,1,n}\).  The dense limit and scaled nondegeneracy imply \(D_n\ge c_\sigma/2\) eventually.  Boundedness also bounds \(R_n\) above.  It follows that
\[
 \frac{\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}}{\sigma_n^2}-1
 =\frac{\rho E_{\tau,1,n}}{D_n}+o_p(1).
\]
The deterministic leading term is nonnegative and bounded.  This proves asymptotic conservativeness and proves the stated if-and-only-if criterion for ratio consistency.

For coverage, take an arbitrary subsequence.  The ratios \(r_n=D_n/R_n\) are bounded away from zero and have limit points in \((0,1]\); pass to a further subsequence on which \(r_n\to r\).  The centered CLT, the preceding variance convergence, and Slutsky's theorem give
\[
 \frac{\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n}{\sqrt{\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}}}
 \rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,r).
\]
Because \(r\le1\), continuity of the normal distribution implies
\[
 \lim\Pr\{\tau_n\in I_{n,\alpha}^{\mathrm{CR2}}\}
 =\Pr\{|\mathcal N(0,r)|\le z_{1-\alpha/2}\}\ge1-\alpha
\]
on that further subsequence.  The subsequence principle proves the asserted global \(\liminf\) coverage, and the same calculation proves the final stated subsequential limit law.

When \(\rho=0\), Theorem~\ref{thm:dense-projection-limit} gives \(G_n\sigma_n^2=R_n+o(1)\), while Theorem~\ref{thm:cr2-phase-frontier} gives \(G_n\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}=R_n+o_p(1)\).  Scaled-variance nondegeneracy makes \(R_n\) bounded away from zero eventually, so
\[
 \widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}/\sigma_n^2\xrightarrow{p}1.
\]
Combining this with Theorem~\ref{thm:centered-design-clt} and Slutsky's theorem proves the displayed standard-normal limit.  The argument used only \(N_n/n\to0\), not \(N_n^2/n\to0\).  For example, after rounding to a multiple of the fixed \(M\), \(N_n\asymp n^{3/4}\) has \(N_n/n\to0\) and \(N_n^2/n\to\infty\), so it is covered.

For a pair \(A=\{j,k\}\), write \(h(A)=(a_j+a_k)/2\).  Among the \(\binom82=28\) pairs, six have value \(1\), six have value \(-1\), and sixteen have value zero.  Thus \(\mathbb E_8h=0\) and
\[
 V_{1,n}=\mathbb E_8h^2=\frac{12}{28}=\frac37.
\]
Moreover \(h(A)=2^{-1}\sum_{i\in A}a_i\) is degree one: averaging it over a disjoint pair gives
\[
 (\mathsf K_8h)(A)=\frac1{6}\sum_{i\notin A}a_i
 =-\frac1{6}\sum_{i\in A}a_i=-\frac13h(A).
\]
Thus \(E_{\tau,1,n}=\|h\|_8^2=3/7\).  Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-kneser-identity} gives \(C_{11,n}=(-1/3)(3/7)=-1/7\), while all control quantities vanish.  Since \(p_n=1/2\), Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-pame-variance} gives
\[
 \sigma_n^2=\frac{(3/7)/(1/2)}4-\frac17-\frac{-1/7}{2}=\frac17
\]
and
\[
 \mathbb E\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}
 =\frac{V_{1,n}-C_{11,n}}{G_{1n}}
 =\frac{3/7+1/7}{2}=\frac27.
\]
There are \((8-1)!!=105\) perfect matchings and \(\binom42=6\) treated-pair choices per matching.  Directly summing \(\widehat\tau_n^2\) and \(\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}\) over these \(630\) equally likely points gives respectively \(630/7\) and \(1260/7\); division by \(630\) reproduces \(1/7\) and \(2/7\).  The estimator mean is zero by sign balance (or by Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-pame-variance}), so the first moment calculation is the variance.

For an additive schedule write \(x_{iz}=Y_{i,n}(z,A)\), independently of \(A\), and \(\bar x_z=n^{-1}\sum_i x_{iz}\).  Then
\[
 h_{z,n}(A)-\bar x_z=\frac1M\sum_{i\in A}(x_{iz}-\bar x_z).
\]
If \(w_i=x_{iz}-\bar x_z\), then \(\sum_iw_i=0\), and direct sampling-without-replacement algebra gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|h_{z,n}^{\circ}\|_n^2
 &=\frac1{M^2}\left\{\frac Mn\sum_iw_i^2
 +\frac{M(M-1)}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i\ne j}w_iw_j\right\}\\
 &=\frac{n-M}{M(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_iw_i^2. \qquad\text{(1)}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Also, conditioning on \(A\), the mean of this centered function over a disjoint \(M\)-set is
\[
 \frac1{n-M}\sum_{i\notin A}w_i
 =-\frac M{n-M}\left(\frac1M\sum_{i\in A}w_i\right).
\]
Thus it lies in Johnson degree one.  Formula (1) consequently applies to the degree-one energy of every additive arm difference.

Under \(\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{same}}\), the empirical variances of both arm arrays converge in prior probability to one, while the arm difference is identically zero.  Under \(\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{ind}}\), the two empirical variances converge to one and the empirical variance of \(U_i-V_i\) converges to two.  These conclusions follow directly from Chebyshev's inequality because the relevant iid variables are bounded and have the stated expectations.  Since \((n-M)/(n-1)\to1\), (1) proves
\[
 V_{1,n},V_{0,n}\longrightarrow\frac1M,\qquad
 E_{\tau,1,n}\longrightarrow
 \begin{cases}0,&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{same}},\\2/M,&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{ind}},\end{cases}
\]
in prior probability.  Because all these additive functions are degree one, Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-kneser-identity} gives \(C_{\tau\tau,n}=\lambda_{n,1}E_{\tau,1,n}\) and \(C_{zz,n}=\lambda_{n,1}V_{z,n}\).  The exact variance identity therefore gives, without invoking nondegeneracy,
\[
 G_n\sigma_n^2
 =R_n+G_n\lambda_{n,1}E_{\tau,1,n}
 -\frac{\lambda_{n,1}V_{1,n}}{p_n}
 -\frac{\lambda_{n,1}V_{0,n}}{1-p_n}.
\]
Now \(\lambda_{n,1}\to0\) and \(G_n\lambda_{n,1}=-N_n/(n-M)\to-\rho\).  Substitution of the preceding prior limits proves the two asserted limits for \(G_n\sigma_n^2\).  Their difference is \(2\rho/M\), and
\[
 \frac1{Mp(1-p)}-\frac{2\rho}{M}
 \ge\frac4M-\frac2M=\frac2M,
\]
using \(p(1-p)\le1/4\) and \(\rho\le1\).  This also proves the stated high-prior-probability nondegeneracy whenever \(c_\sigma\) is strictly below the smaller limit.

It remains to compare observations.  Conditional on any realized \((\mathbf A_n,\mathbf Z_n)\), each sampled unit is observed in exactly one arm.  Under the common prior its observation is its independent sign \(U_i\); under the independent prior it is \(U_i\) in a treated group and \(V_i\) in a control group.  In either case the entire vector of observed individual outcomes consists of independent Rademacher variables and is independent of the design.  Unit labels, groups, and treatment labels have the same design law under both priors.  Hence the induced laws of \(\mathcal O_n\) are exactly equal.

theorem.statement:
Fix \(M\ge2\), \(p\in(0,1)\), \(\rho\in(0,1]\), \(B\ge1\), and design sequences satisfying the three fraction and growth assumptions.  Put
\[
 d_{\mathrm{same}}=\frac1{Mp(1-p)},\qquad
 d_{\mathrm{ind}}=\frac1{Mp(1-p)}-\frac{2\rho}{M},
\]
and suppose \(0<c_\sigma<d_{\mathrm{ind}}\).  There are high-prior-probability sets of deterministic Rademacher schedule rows whose Cartesian diagonal selections all belong to \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{dense}}\); after conditioning \(\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{same}}\) and \(\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{ind}}\) on these sets, their induced one-realization mixture laws have total-variation distance tending to zero, while \(G_n\sigma_n^2\) converges uniformly on the respective supports to \(d_{\mathrm{same}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{ind}}\).  Consequently there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that every measurable \(\widehat S_n(\mathcal O_n)\) obeys
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\sup_{Y\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{dense}}}
 \Pr_Y\left(\left|\frac{\widehat S_n}{\sigma_n^2}-1\right|>\varepsilon\right)
 \ge\frac12.
\]
Thus no estimator from one realization is uniformly ratio-consistent for the exact variance over the full dense class.  The deterministic support arrays, rather than a generally unavailable pair of deterministic arrays with close laws, are the valid diagonal certificate.
theorem.proof_tex:
Let \(j\in\{\mathrm{same},\mathrm{ind}\}\).  Proposition~\ref{prop:rademacher-mixture-separation} and Lemma~\ref{lem:rademacher-predictable-variation} imply the following for every fixed integer \(k\): with \(\mathbb H_n^j\)-probability tending to one,
\[
 |G_n\sigma_n^2-d_j|\le k^{-1}
\]
and, for every \(1\le m\le k\),
\[
 \mathbb P_{\mathbf A_n,\mathbf Z_n}
 \left(|Q_n/\sigma_n^2-1|>m^{-1}\mid Y\right)\le k^{-1}.
\]
The elementary diagonal lemma therefore supplies integers \(k_n\uparrow\infty\) slowly enough that the set \(\Gamma_n^j\) on which all these inequalities hold with \(k=k_n\) satisfies \(\mathbb H_n^j(\Gamma_n^j)\to1\).  Every schedule in these sets is bounded by one.  Every deterministic selection \(Y_n\in\Gamma_n^j\) has \(G_n\sigma_n^2\to d_j>c_\sigma\); and for fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), choosing \(m\) with \(m^{-1}<\varepsilon\) in the second display proves \(Q_n/\sigma_n^2\xrightarrow{p}1\).  The deterministic design sequences already satisfy growth and the two fraction limits.  Hence every Cartesian diagonal selection belongs to \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{dense}}\).  This also supplies the requested deterministic-array selection without claiming that one fixed pair of deterministic arrays must itself have close observation laws.

Let \(\widetilde{\mathbb H}_n^j\) be \(\mathbb H_n^j\) conditioned on \(\Gamma_n^j\), and let \(P_n^j\) be its induced law of \(\mathcal O_n\).  Conditioning changes a prior by total variation \(\mathbb H_n^j((\Gamma_n^j)^c)=o(1)\), and passage through the design-and-observation kernel cannot increase total variation.  The two unconditioned observation mixtures are exactly equal by Proposition~\ref{prop:rademacher-mixture-separation}.  The triangle inequality consequently gives
\[
 \|P_n^{\mathrm{same}}-P_n^{\mathrm{ind}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=o(1). \qquad\text{(9)}
\]
At the same time, by construction,
\[
 \sup_{Y\in\Gamma_n^j}|G_n\sigma_n^2(Y)-d_j|\le k_n^{-1}. \qquad\text{(10)}
\]

Write \(a=d_{\mathrm{same}}\), \(b=d_{\mathrm{ind}}\), and \(\Delta=a-b=2\rho/M>0\).  Choose \(0<\varepsilon<\Delta/(4a)\), and test the two conditioned hypotheses by declaring ``same'' exactly when
\[
 G_n\widehat S_n>(a+b)/2.
\]
By (10), for all sufficiently large \(n\), relative error at most \(\varepsilon\) forces the correct declaration under either hypothesis.  Therefore the sum of the two testing-error probabilities is no larger than the sum of the two mixture probabilities of relative estimation error exceeding \(\varepsilon\).  Conversely, the elementary testing inequality
\[
 P_n^{\mathrm{same}}(\text{error})+P_n^{\mathrm{ind}}(\text{error})
 \ge1-\|P_n^{\mathrm{same}}-P_n^{\mathrm{ind}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\]
follows directly by writing the two errors for the test's decision set.  By (9), the maximum of the two mixture estimation risks is at least \(1/2-o(1)\) at every \(n\).  Each mixture is supported on rows extendible to arrays in \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{dense}}\), so each average risk, and therefore their maximum, is bounded above by the displayed supremum over that class.  Taking the lower limit proves the claimed bound and rules out uniform ratio consistency.

added_lemmas.statement: For the Kneser graph on the \(M\)-subsets of an \(n\)-set, where adjacency means disjointness and \(n\ge2M\), the unnormalized adjacency eigenvalue on \(\mathcal H_{n,k}\) is \((-1)^k\binom{n-M-k}{M-k}\), for \(0\le k\le M\).

source.verbatim_statement: Proposition 3.1. (Lovasz [23]) The eigenvalues of the Kneser graph are \(P_{id}=(-1)^i\binom{n-d-i}{d-i}=(-1)^i\binom{n-d-i}{n-2d}\).

added_lemmas.statement: On the uniform \(M\)-slice with \(n\ge2M\), the Johnson harmonic degree spaces \(\mathcal H_{n,0},\ldots,\mathcal H_{n,M}\) form an orthogonal direct-sum decomposition of \(L^2(\Omega_{n,M})\).

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(D_{n,r}\) be a square-integrable martingale-difference triangular array adapted to \(\mathcal F_{n,r}\), let \(\sigma_n>0\), and put \(Q_n=\sum_r\mathbb E[D_{n,r}^2\mid\mathcal F_{n,r-1}]\).  If \(Q_n/\sigma_n^2\xrightarrow{p}1\) and, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
 \sigma_n^{-2}\sum_r\mathbb E\!\left[D_{n,r}^2
 \mathbf 1\{|D_{n,r}|>\varepsilon\sigma_n\}\mid\mathcal F_{n,r-1}\right]
 \xrightarrow{p}0,
\]
then \(\sigma_n^{-1}\sum_rD_{n,r}\rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,1)\).

added_lemmas.statement:
Suppose \(G_n\to\infty\), \(p_n\to p\in(0,1)\), and \(N_n/n\to\rho\in[0,1]\).  Under either \(\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{same}}\) or \(\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{ind}}\), the unit-permutation-then-label-permutation predictable variation satisfies, jointly over the prior and design,
\[
 G_nQ_n\xrightarrow{L^2}
 \begin{cases}
 [Mp(1-p)]^{-1},&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{same}},\\
 [Mp(1-p)]^{-1}-2\rho/M,&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{ind}}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Consequently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), under either prior,
\[
 \mathbb P_{\mathbb H_n}\!\left\{
 \mathbb P_{\mathbf A_n,\mathbf Z_n}\!\left(
 \left|Q_n/\sigma_n^2-1\right|>\varepsilon\mid Y\right)>\varepsilon
 \right\}\longrightarrow0.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
We compute the predictable variation for the stipulated filtration.  Put \(q_n=1-p_n\), \(d_i=x_{i1}-x_{i0}\), and, for realized block \(A_g\),
\[
 c_g=\frac{h_{1,n}(A_g)}{p_n}+\frac{h_{0,n}(A_g)}{q_n}.
\]
Averaging first over the treatment labels shows that the martingale at unit-reveal time \(N_n\) equals the simple-random-sample mean \(N_n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N_n}d_{U_j}\), centered at \(n^{-1}\sum_id_i\).  The remaining label-randomization residual is
\[
 \frac1{G_n}\sum_{g=1}^{G_n}(Z_g-p_n)c_g. \qquad\text{(2)}
\]
Thus \(Q_n=Q_n^U+Q_n^L\), the sums of conditional variances over the two consecutive reveal phases.

Let \(\mu_{r-1}^d\) and \(v_{r-1}^d\) be the mean and the denominator-population variance of the \(n-r+1\) unit values remaining just before unit reveal \(r\).  If \(N_n<n\), direct subtraction of the two successive conditional sample means gives
\[
 D_{n,r}^U=\frac{n-N_n}{N_n(n-r)}(d_{U_r}-\mu_{r-1}^d),\qquad
 Q_n^U=\sum_{r=1}^{N_n}\frac{(n-N_n)^2}{N_n^2(n-r)^2}v_{r-1}^d. \qquad\text{(3)}
\]
If \(N_n=n\), this phase is identically zero.  Under the common prior \(d_i=0\).  Under the independent prior the permuted \(d_i\) are iid, bounded, mean zero, and variance two.  If \(\rho<1\), all remaining populations in (3) have order \(n\), and the elementary bound \(\mathbb E|v_{r-1}^d-2|\le C(n-r+1)^{-1/2}\), obtained by expanding the empirical first two moments, applies.  Moreover, with \(L_n=n-N_n\),
\[
 G_n\sum_{r=1}^{N_n}\frac{L_n^2}{N_n^2(n-r)^2}
 =\frac{L_n^2}{MN_n}\sum_{j=L_n}^{n-1}j^{-2}\longrightarrow\frac{1-\rho}{M}. \qquad\text{(4)}
\]
If \(\rho=1\) and \(L_n\ge1\), the left side of (4) is at most \((1+L_n)/(MN_n)\to0\); it is zero when \(L_n=0\).  Equations (3)--(4) therefore give
\[
 G_nQ_n^U\xrightarrow{L^1}
 \begin{cases}0,&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{same}},\\2(1-\rho)/M,&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{ind}}.\end{cases} \qquad\text{(5)}
\]

For the label phase, let \(s\) labels have been exposed, let
\[
 \pi_{s-1}=\frac{G_{1n}-\sum_{j<s}Z_j}{G_n-s+1},\qquad
 \bar c_{s+1:G_n}=\frac1{G_n-s}\sum_{j>s}c_j.
\]
Subtracting successive conditional expectations in (2) gives, for \(s<G_n\),
\[
 D_{n,N_n+s}^L=\frac{Z_s-\pi_{s-1}}{G_n}
 (c_s-\bar c_{s+1:G_n}),
\]
and the final increment is zero.  Hence
\[
 G_nQ_n^L=\frac1{G_n}\sum_{s=1}^{G_n-1}
 \pi_{s-1}(1-\pi_{s-1})(c_s-\bar c_{s+1:G_n})^2. \qquad\text{(6)}
\]
The label process is independent of the \(c_g\)'s.  If \(L=G_n-s+1\), direct hypergeometric covariance algebra gives
\[
 \mathbb E(\pi_{s-1}-p_n)^2
 =p_nq_n\frac{G_n-L}{L(G_n-1)}.
\]
Since \(|x(1-x)-p_nq_n|\le2|x-p_n|\), averaging the square roots of these variances over \(L=2,\ldots,G_n\) shows that replacing every weight in (6) by \(p_nq_n\) changes (6) by \(o_{L^1}(1)\); boundedness of \(c_g\) is uniform because \(p_n,q_n\) are eventually bounded away from zero.

Under either prior the disjoint blocks contain independent prior signs, so \(c_1,\ldots,c_{G_n}\) are iid, bounded, and centered.  The reverse updating identity
\[
 \sum_{s=1}^{G_n-1}\frac{G_n-s}{G_n-s+1}
 (c_s-\bar c_{s+1:G_n})^2
 =\sum_{g=1}^{G_n}(c_g-\bar c)^2. \qquad\text{(7)}
\]
is obtained by expanding both sides recursively.  The difference between the unweighted sum on the left of (7) and its weighted version is \(O(\log G_n)\), because \(c_g\) is uniformly bounded.  The iid law of large numbers applied to the right side therefore shows that the unweighted average in (6) converges in \(L^1\) to \(\operatorname{Var}(c_1)\).  Now
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(c_1)=
 \begin{cases}
 [Mp_n^2q_n^2]^{-1},&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{same}},\\
 M^{-1}(p_n^{-2}+q_n^{-2}),&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{ind}}.
 \end{cases}
\]
It follows from (6) that
\[
 G_nQ_n^L\xrightarrow{L^1}
 \begin{cases}
 [Mpq]^{-1},&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{same}},\\
 M^{-1}(q/p+p/q),&\mathbb H_n^{\mathrm{ind}}.
 \end{cases} \qquad\text{(8)}
\]
Adding (5) and (8), and using \(q/p+p/q+2=1/(pq)\), proves the two asserted constants.  Indeed, the coefficient sum in (4) is at most \(1/M\), because it contains \(N_n\) terms and each is at most \(L_n^{-2}\), and (6) is bounded by the uniform envelope for \(c_g^2\).  Thus all scaled quantities in (3) and (6) are uniformly bounded; the \(L^1\) convergence upgrades to \(L^2\).  In particular, \(\operatorname{Var}(G_nQ_n)=o(1)\), which is the requested normalized-variance check.

Proposition~\ref{prop:rademacher-mixture-separation} gives convergence in prior probability of \(G_n\sigma_n^2\) to the same strictly positive constants.  Thus \(Q_n/\sigma_n^2\to1\) jointly in prior and design probability.  If
\[
 b_n(Y)=\mathbb P_{\mathbf A_n,\mathbf Z_n}
 \left(|Q_n/\sigma_n^2-1|>\varepsilon\mid Y\right),
\]
then joint convergence says \(\mathbb E_{\mathbb H_n}b_n(Y)\to0\).  Markov's inequality gives \(\mathbb P_{\mathbb H_n}\{b_n(Y)>\varepsilon\}\to0\), proving the final assertion.

proposed.statement: For every \(n\ge2M\), \(\mathsf K_n\) acts on \(\mathcal H_{n,k}\) by \(\lambda_{n,k}=(-1)^k(M)_k/(n-M)_k\). Consequently, for centered \(f,g\in L^2(\Omega_{n,M})\) and a uniform ordered disjoint pair \((A,C)\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(f(A),g(C))=\sum_{k=1}^M\lambda_{n,k}\langle\Pi_{n,k}f,\Pi_{n,k}g\rangle_n\), and \(C_{\tau\tau,n}=\sum_{k=1}^M\lambda_{n,k}\|\Pi_{n,k}(h_{1,n}-h_{0,n})\|_n^2\).
proposed.justification: This identity converts the global dependence from disjoint group formation into auditable harmonic energies with exact signs and finite-sample constants.
proposed.gap: Filmus2016, Theorem 3 and the Johnson-scheme discussion, supplies the common eigenspaces, while BrouwerEtAl2018 supplies the classical Kneser spectrum; neither derives a causal design variance for random groups.
proposed.consumer: The identity is the input for the dense PAME variance correction and every subsequent comparison with CR2.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The exact spectrum is classical substrate and must be declared as a cited leaf in the theorem's direct proof spine.

proposed.statement: For every triangular array in \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{dense}}\), \[\frac{\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n}{\sigma_n}\rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,1).\] The only randomness is \((\mathbf A_n,\mathbf Z_n)\); the composition-indexed potential outcomes are fixed, and the Lindeberg condition is derived in \(\mathrm{Lemma}~\ref{lem:reveal-increment-bound}\) rather than assumed.
proposed.justification: Centered Gaussian inference survives dense global dependence when the actual reveal martingale has stable predictable variation.
proposed.gap: LiDing2017, Theorem 4, handles complete treatment randomization conditional on fixed experimental units; Ohlsson1989 handles conventional two-stage sampling; neither covers composition-indexed scores generated by a positive-fraction disjoint partition.
proposed.consumer: The result supplies design-based normal inference for PAME when independent-group coupling is asymptotically invalid.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof invokes the classical martingale triangular-array CLT and the exact centering result directly, so both are made explicit dependencies.

proposed.statement: If the same conditions hold with \(\rho=0\), then \[\frac{\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n}{\sqrt{\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}}}\rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,1)\] under \(N_n/n\to0\), with no condition on \(N_n^2/n\). This replaces the whole-tuple birthday condition in FuSamiiWang2026, Theorems 1--2, by the statistic-specific predictable-variation condition and includes sequences such as \(N_n=n^{3/4}\), for which \(N_n^2/n\to\infty\).
proposed.justification: Scalar PAME inference needs a vanishing sampling fraction, not a vanishing whole-tuple collision probability.
proposed.gap: FuSamiiWang2026 imposes the birthday-scale restriction \(N_n^2/n\to0\) because its proof couples the entire group tuple, while this theorem targets only the scalar statistic.
proposed.consumer: Experiments grouping \(n^{3/4}\) of \(n\) eligible units obtain justified CR2 inference despite failure of whole-design coupling.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof uses scaled-variance nondegeneracy and the dense projection limit directly, so the sparse corollary's dependency metadata is made explicit.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a realized data set and suppress the row index \(n\).  The equality to be proved is deterministic conditional on these data.  For a realized group \(g\) in arm \(z\), let \(y_g\in\mathbb R^M\) be its vector of individual observed outcomes, let \(\mathbf 1_M\) be the \(M\)-vector of ones, and put
\[
 H_g=M^{-1}\mathbf 1_M^{\mathsf T}y_g=H^{\mathrm{obs}}_{ng},
 \qquad x_z=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ z\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad X_g=\mathbf 1_M x_z^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Thus the rows of \(X_g\) are precisely the intercept and numeric binary-treatment regressors specified in the proposition.  Write \(G_z=G_{zn}\), so that \(G_1=G_{1n}\) and \(G_0=G_{0n}\).  Because \(M>0\) and both \(G_0\) and \(G_1\) are positive, the stacked design matrix \(X\) has rank two.  Direct multiplication gives
\[
 X^{\mathsf T}X
 =M\begin{pmatrix}G_0+G_1&G_1\\G_1&G_1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 B:=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}
 =\frac1M\begin{pmatrix}
 G_0^{-1}&-G_0^{-1}\\
 -G_0^{-1}&G_0^{-1}+G_1^{-1}
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
In particular, if \(c=(0,1)^{\mathsf T}\) selects the treatment coefficient, then
\[
 c^{\mathsf T}Bx_1=\frac{1}{MG_1},
 \qquad
 c^{\mathsf T}Bx_0=-\frac{1}{MG_0}.
 \tag{1}
\]

For an unweighted \({\tt lm}\) object, the documented default working target is the identity matrix, and the documented \({\tt type}={\tt 'CR2'}\), \({\tt form}={\tt 'sandwich'}\) construction is
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_{\mathrm{CR2}}
 =B\sum_{g=1}^{G_0+G_1}
 X_g^{\mathsf T}A_g e_g e_g^{\mathsf T}A_g^{\mathsf T}X_gB,
 \qquad
 A_g=\bigl(I_M-X_gBX_g^{\mathsf T}\bigr)^{-1/2},
 \tag{2}
\]
where \(e_g=y_g-X_g\widehat\beta\) is the ordinary least-squares residual vector; this is the \({\tt vcovCR.lm}\), \({\tt CR2}\), and sandwich construction recorded in \cite{ClubSandwich2026}.  The implementation's bread and scale factors cancel to the matrix \(B\) on both sides of the sum in (2), so (2) is on the usual covariance scale.

Let
\[
 P_M=M^{-1}\mathbf 1_M\mathbf 1_M^{\mathsf T}.
\]
For a group in arm \(z\), the displayed formula for \(B\) yields
\[
 X_gBX_g^{\mathsf T}
 =\mathbf 1_M(x_z^{\mathsf T}Bx_z)\mathbf 1_M^{\mathsf T}
 =G_z^{-1}P_M.
 \tag{3}
\]
The orthogonal projection \(P_M\) is the identity on the cluster-constant subspace and is zero on its orthogonal complement.  Consequently \(I_M-G_z^{-1}P_M\) has eigenvalue \(1-G_z^{-1}>0\) on the cluster-constant subspace and eigenvalue \(1\) on its orthogonal complement.  Positivity follows here from the proposed domain condition \(G_z\ge2\).  Taking the unique symmetric positive-definite inverse square root in (2) therefore gives
\[
 A_g=(I_M-P_M)+a_zP_M,
 \qquad
 a_z=\left(1-\frac1{G_z}\right)^{-1/2}
 =\sqrt{\frac{G_z}{G_z-1}}.
 \tag{4}
\]

Equal group size and the two-regressor design imply, by substituting the displayed inverse \(B\) into \(\widehat\beta=BX^{\mathsf T}y\), that
\[
 \widehat\beta
 =\begin{pmatrix}\bar H_0\\ \bar H_1-\bar H_0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \bar H_z=G_z^{-1}\sum_{g:Z_{ng}=z}H_g.
 \tag{5}
\]
It follows from (5) that the mean residual in group \(g\) is
\[
 M^{-1}\mathbf 1_M^{\mathsf T}e_g=H_g-\bar H_z=:d_g.
 \tag{6}
\]
Equations (4) and (6) then show that within-group residual components orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1_M\) make no contribution to the cluster score and that
\[
 \mathbf 1_M^{\mathsf T}A_ge_g
 =a_z\mathbf 1_M^{\mathsf T}e_g
 =Ma_zd_g.
 \tag{7}
\]
Combining (1) and (7), the treatment-coordinate adjusted score of group \(g\) is exactly
\[
 q_g:=c^{\mathsf T}BX_g^{\mathsf T}A_ge_g
 =\begin{cases}
 a_1d_g/G_1,&Z_{ng}=1,\\
 -a_0d_g/G_0,&Z_{ng}=0.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{8}
\]
Taking the treatment-coordinate entry of (2), using (8), and then using the definition of \(s_{z,n}^2\) in \({\rm def:cr2\text{-}statistic}\), we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 c^{\mathsf T}\widehat\Sigma_{\mathrm{CR2}}c
 &=\sum_g q_g^2\\
 &=\sum_{z=0}^1\frac{a_z^2}{G_z^2}
   \sum_{g:Z_{ng}=z}(H_g-\bar H_z)^2\\
 &=\sum_{z=0}^1
   \frac{G_z}{G_z-1}\frac{(G_z-1)s_{z,n}^2}{G_z^2}\\
 &=\frac{s_{1,n}^2}{G_{1n}}+\frac{s_{0,n}^2}{G_{0n}}
 =\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The last equality is exactly \({\rm def:cr2\text{-}statistic}\).  This proves the claimed software-to-statistic identity.  Notice that no probabilistic independence or outcome-model assumption enters the calculation: \({\rm def:random\text{-}partition\text{-}design}\) supplies the realized equal-size groups and fixed arm counts, while the identity itself holds for every realized outcome array.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: Suppose \(G_{1n}\ge 2\) and \(G_{0n}\ge 2\). Let \({\tt fit}={\tt lm}(Y^{\mathrm{obs}}\sim Z)\) be unweighted, with only an intercept and numeric binary group treatment, equal group size \(M\), and clusters equal the realized groups. With the default identity target, the treatment-coordinate entry of \({\tt clubSandwich::vcovCR}({\tt fit},\ {\tt cluster}={\tt group},\ {\tt type}={\tt 'CR2'})\) equals \(\widehat V_{\mathrm{CR2},n}=s_{1,n}^2/G_{1n}+s_{0,n}^2/G_{0n}\) exactly.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The frozen design permits an arm to contain only one group. In that case the displayed within-arm sample variance divides by zero, and the cluster-constant eigenvalue of the residual-maker block is zero, so the ordinary inverse-square-root CR2 adjustment used in the claimed identity is not defined. Requiring at least two groups in each arm is the minimal finite-sample domain condition and is automatic eventually under the paper's treatment-fraction and group-growth assumptions.
